proposals.quote_modern: He doubted whether to embrace him
proposals.replacement: He did not know whether to embrace him
proposals.butler: He doubted whether to embrace him, kiss him, and tell him all about his having come home, or whether he should first question him and see what he would say.
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier ¶14 'He doubted whether to embrace him' (word, pause, high): "'Doubted whether' = couldn't decide whether (old usage)." Book-level note 6 lists 'doubted whether' among the Book's archaisms.
proposals.reason: This is a dead sense. Today 'doubt whether' means to question whether something is so, so 'He doubted whether to embrace him' reads as reluctance to embrace his father. Butler's sense is being torn between two courses, which the 'or whether' that follows spells out. No current modern Book keeps Butler's 'doubted whether'. The same construction ('he doubted whether to …, or to …') is printed 'he did not know whether to …, or to …' at 4.9. 6.11 prints 'did not know what to do' (GLOSSARY Book 5/6 table, B06-P012) and 10.11 'was uncertain whether'. 'did not know whether' follows 4.9 exactly and leaves GLOSSARY's reserved 'still undecided' alone. Three words replace two, and every clause stays in Butler's order. The reader recovered, so this is optional.
proposals.collision_check: Butler's ¶14 has no 'know'. His 'did not see Dolius' uses 'did not' in the same plain negating job. 'deemed it best' is already the GLOSSARY's 'thought it best' and is unaffected. 'still undecided' (reserved for 'thus in two minds') is not used.

proposals.quote_modern: but bears the trace of your attention
proposals.replacement: that does not bear the trace of your attention
proposals.butler: There is not a single plant, not a fig tree, vine, olive, pear, nor flower bed, but bears the trace of your attention.
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier ¶15 on the whole sentence (syntax, pause, high): "Every plant shows your care. The 'not a single ... but' construction can be misread as 'no plant shows your care'." Note: 'Archaic double negative.'
proposals.reason: This is obsolete syntax that can invert the sense. 'not a single X … but bears' (meaning 'that does not bear') is no longer current English, where 'but' reads as 'except' or as a contrast. So the sentence can be taken as 'no plant bears the trace of your attention', the opposite of Odysseus's compliment. 'that does not bear' is the current form of the same double negative. Every item Butler lists stays, in his order, and nothing is added or dropped. The next sentence ('you take better care of your garden than of yourself') lets an attentive reader recover, so this is optional. The accepted record already modernized the same class at 23.11 (Butler's 'even though he was not one who would leave many friends').
proposals.collision_check: Butler's ¶15 uses 'not' throughout in the same negating job, and 'that' repeatedly as a relative and conjunction ('this place that I have come to'). There is no 'does' in his ¶15, and 'bear' is his own verb, kept. No Butler word is reused for something else.

proposals.quote_modern: with corn planted between each row
proposals.replacement: with grain planted between each row
proposals.butler: there was corn planted between each row
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier ¶20 'with corn planted between each row' (word, MISREAD, medium): "Grain (wheat or barley). American readers will picture maize, which is out of place here."
proposals.reason: This is a transatlantic false friend. Butler's British 'corn' means grain in general. This edition is American English throughout (GLOSSARY spelling standard), and in American English 'corn' is maize, a New World crop. So the ordinary reader pictures maize growing between Laertes's vines and never notices that anything is wrong. The package has already made this rendering: 3.36 prints 'the grain lands of the open country' for Butler's 'the corn lands'. One word changes and nothing is added. Butler's claim that a crop was sown between the vine rows stands.
proposals.collision_check: Butler's ¶20 has no 'grain'. His 'grapes' ('yield grapes of every kind') is a different word and stays. No other Butler word is displaced.

proposals.butler: making him taller and stouter than before
proposals.reader_evidence: Barrier ¶23 'making him taller and stouter than before' (word, pause, high): "Sturdier and more robust, not fatter." Note: "In modern English 'stout' usually means fat."
proposals.reason: This is a false friend, and the proposal keeps one Butler phrase to one rendering across Books. Of a person's build, current 'stout' chiefly means portly, so as Athena gives Laertes 'a more imposing presence', a typical reader has her make him fatter. Butler means solidly built (the Greek comparative is 'thicker-set, sturdier'), and 'sturdier' keeps his meaning and his comparative. The Book 8 adjudication proposes the same change for Butler's same phrase at 8.1 (B08-01, 'taller and sturdier', optional) and names 24.23 as the other instance. Apply this together with B08-01 or not at all, so that one Butler phrase keeps one rendering. It is optional because the reader recovered. Butler's different phrase at 23.15, 'taller and stronger', is left alone and stays distinct.
proposals.collision_check: Butler's ¶23 has 'taller' twice ('taller and stouter', and 'much taller and better-looking' in Odysseus's remark), and both stay. 'sturdy' occurs nowhere in Butler's ¶23. His 'stronger' at 23.15 is in another paragraph and is not touched.

rejected_barriers.quote: Then Hermes of Cyllene summoned the ghosts of the suitors
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's opening and epithet ('Mercury of Cyllene', name-mapped). The cut to the underworld is the poem's own, and the paragraph shows Hermes guiding the dead. Not explained.

rejected_barriers.quote: the waters of Oceanus and the rock Leucas, they came to the gates of the sun and the land of dreams
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's mythic geography. The reader got the gist (a journey beyond the living world). Not explained.

rejected_barriers.quote: the meadow of asphodel
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's term, first met in Book 11. The sentence itself says what the meadow is ('where the souls and shadows of those who can labor no more dwell'). Read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: the Danaans
rejected_barriers.reason: Ethnic name, kept unglossed by instruction.

rejected_barriers.quote: after Peleus’s son himself
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's patronymic for Achilles, who is named a line earlier. Read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: They gathered around the ghost of Peleus’s son
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's 'They gathered round the ghost of the son of Peleus'. The unmarked subject and the order of the scene are Butler's and Homer's: the arrival is told in ¶0–1, the exchange follows in ¶2–6, and the suitors approach in ¶7. Reordering is excluded, and the reader resolved it correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: those who had died with him in Aegisthus’s house
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's words. ¶6 and ¶11 supply the rest, and the Agamemnon story is told in Books 1, 3, 4 and 11.

rejected_barriers.quote: Son of Atreus
rejected_barriers.reason: Patronymic, kept by instruction. ¶9 names Agamemnon with it.

rejected_barriers.quote: Fortunate son of Peleus,” replied Agamemnon’s ghost, “for dying at Troy
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's exclamation ('Happy son of Peleus … for having died at Troy'), with his speech tag in the same place. It is not the split vocative PUNCTUATION.md §3 normalizes, because the tag does not fall between an adjective and its noun. Read correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: far from Argos
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's words: 'Argos' as home ground is the poem's usage. Not resolved.

rejected_barriers.quote: fighting for your body
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's words, read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: mighty in your might, no longer troubled about your prowess in battle
rejected_barriers.reason: The accepted rendering of Butler's 'all huge and hugely, heedless now of your chivalry'. It is faithful and was read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: Hold fast, Argives, do not flee, sons of the Achaeans
rejected_barriers.reason: Ethnic names, kept unglossed by instruction.

rejected_barriers.quote: The daughters of the old man of the sea
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's words. Not explained.

rejected_barriers.quote: with the tramp of a great multitude
rejected_barriers.reason: 'tramp' (heavy tread) is current, and the reader read it correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: when the flames of heaven had done their work
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's words. The pyre has just been described, and the reader took this as the pyre fire.

rejected_barriers.quote: a gift from Dionysus and the work of Hephaestus himself
rejected_barriers.reason: The gods appear under the edition's name forms (Butler's Bacchus and Vulcan), and by instruction their roles are not explained. The reader understood the urn as divine. There is a records note in recurring: the GLOSSARY supplied here has no Bacchus row.

rejected_barriers.quote: separately we enclosed those of Antilochus
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's 'separate we enclosed also those of Antilochus'. Butler does not name the container either.

rejected_barriers.quote: the open Hellespont
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's place name, read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: when young men gird themselves
rejected_barriers.reason: 'gird oneself' is dignified but current, and it was read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: silver-footed Thetis
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's epithet, read correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: at the hands of Aegisthus and my wicked wife
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's words. The adultery is backstory from Books 1, 3, 4 and 11.

rejected_barriers.quote: presently Hermes came up to them with the ghosts of the suitors
rejected_barriers.reason: Ruling: keep 'presently'. In past narration it can only mean 'soon after', and the reader glossed it so. The ordering of ¶0–7 is Butler's and Homer's and is not rearranged.

rejected_barriers.quote: all of an age too
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's idiom, current if literary. Read correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: cattle-lifting
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's compound for cattle-raiding, read correctly with high confidence. The GLOSSARY 'oxen' row concerns Odysseus's herds and does not reach this compound.

rejected_barriers.quote: or fighting to defend their wives and city
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's 'or while fighting in defence of their wives and city' has the same open 'their'. Resolving it would be interpretation.

rejected_barriers.quote: Sweethearts
rejected_barriers.reason: Ruling: keep. This is Butler's own address to the suitors in Penelope's speech. The reader identified the addressees correctly, and the tone they hear (sweetness, as a resentful suitor reports it) is within Butler's. The same speech recurs in Books 2 and 19, so any change would have to be made in all three places together. It is a question of tone, not a comprehension repair.

rejected_barriers.quote: for I would not have my skill in needlework perish unrecorded
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's words, including his clause set off by dashes. The reader's reading (she does not want her work wasted) is right, and the link to 'wait' is Butler's.

rejected_barriers.quote: a pall for the hero Laertes
rejected_barriers.reason: Ruling on the weaving nouns: keep. 'pall' is current (as in 'pallbearer'), and the sentence explains it ('ready for the time when death takes him … laid out without a pall'). The reader read it correctly with high confidence. Laertes is Odysseus's father from Book 1 on.

rejected_barriers.quote: her great web
rejected_barriers.reason: Ruling on the weaving nouns: keep. 'needlework', 'pall', 'web', 'stitches' and 'robe' are Butler's own distinct nouns for the work and the finished cloth ('tambour frame' is already 'embroidery frame'). Merging them would render several Butler words with one (D26). 'working on her great web all day long' and 'unpick the stitches' fix 'web' as cloth, and the reader read it that way.

rejected_barriers.quote: offer his bow and a quantity of iron to be competed for
rejected_barriers.reason: Ruling: not a defect of the modernization. The modern repeats Butler: 'offer his bow and a quantity of iron to be contended for', then 'sent his arrow through the iron'. The iron is the row of axes the contest was set with in Books 19 and 21, and Butler does not name them here either, so nothing he identifies here has been lost. This is Amphimedon's speech, where no gloss is allowed, and recasting 'to be competed for' as an instrument would rewrite Butler's wording. The paraphrase ('a contest with his bow and some iron') is right.

rejected_barriers.quote: aegis-bearing Zeus
rejected_barriers.reason: GLOSSARY epithet ('aegis' kept unglossed).

rejected_barriers.quote: took the weapons and hid them in an inner room
rejected_barriers.reason: Backstory from Books 16 and 19 (clearing the arms from the hall). Read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: stood on the floor of the gallery and poured his arrows on the ground
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's words, with the GLOSSARY's 'gallery' for 'cloister'. Read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: for they fell upon us with might and main
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's 'they' (Odysseus and his helpers, a god among them) and his idiom 'with might and main', current if dated. Read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: Fortunate Odysseus, son of Laertes,” replied Agamemnon’s ghost
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's apostrophe to the absent Odysseus ('Happy Ulysses, son of Laertes'). Read correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: the daughter of Tyndareus, who killed her lawful husband
rejected_barriers.reason: Patronymic, kept by instruction. ¶6 has already said that Agamemnon's wife killed him, and the reader connected the two.

rejected_barriers.quote: which he had reclaimed with endless labor
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's 'reclaimed' (brought into cultivation) is current, as in 'reclaimed land'. Read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: a lean-to running all around it
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's words, read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: an old Sicel woman
rejected_barriers.reason: Ethnic name, kept unglossed by instruction.

rejected_barriers.quote: he did not see Dolius, nor any of his sons nor the other bondservants
rejected_barriers.reason: Dolius is named in earlier Books (Book 4), and ¶25 gives his household here. 'bondservants' renders Butler's 'bondsmen'. It is the edition's settled word (the Book 4 adjudication keeps it), and D26 keeps it apart from his 'slaves' (¶12, ¶15).

rejected_barriers.quote: at the place where the old man had told them
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's words, with the same open referent. Resolving it would be interpretation.

rejected_barriers.quote: bound round with thongs of oxhide
rejected_barriers.reason: 'thongs' (leather strips) is current, and the sentence says what they are for. Read correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: It cannot be because you are idle that your master takes such poor care of you
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's words. The pretense is Odysseus's and is not explained.

rejected_barriers.quote: his father was Laertes, son of Arceisius
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's lie and patronymic. ¶14 ('to be crafty with him') announces the deception, and by instruction the poem's lies are not flagged.

rejected_barriers.quote: seven talents of fine gold
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's unit, read correctly with high confidence. It is in dialogue, where no gloss is allowed.

rejected_barriers.quote: twelve cloaks of single fold, twelve rugs, twelve fair mantles
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's list, kept item by item (GLOSSARY: concrete detail is kept exactly). Read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: four good-looking women skilled in all useful arts, and I let him take his choice
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's words, read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: my unhappy son, if ever there was one
rejected_barriers.reason: A current idiom for Butler's 'as ever was', read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: his excellent and richly dowered wife
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's phrase. The reader's reading (a match with great wealth attached) is within Butler's sense.

rejected_barriers.quote: quite truthfully
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's 'quite truly'. The lie is the poem's, and by instruction it is not flagged.

rejected_barriers.quote: The birds all flew on our right hands
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's words. The sentence before says 'the omens were good'. Read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: He filled both hands with dust from the ground and poured it over his gray head
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's mourning gesture, read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: his nostrils quivered
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's image, read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: as I followed you around the garden
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's words. Butler does not say Odysseus was a child, and adding it would add content.

rejected_barriers.quote: then you gods are still on Olympus after all
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's words, read correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: throughout the cities of the Cephallenians
rejected_barriers.reason: Ethnic name, kept unglossed by instruction.

rejected_barriers.quote: the stockman and the swineherd
rejected_barriers.reason: Philoetius and Eumaeus, introduced in earlier Books. Butler names them by trade here.

rejected_barriers.quote: his son was surprised to see him
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's words, read correctly (the son is Odysseus).

rejected_barriers.quote: took Nericum, that strong fortress on the foreland
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's 'foreland' is current geographic English and was read correctly. It stays apart from 'headland' (24.6, for Butler's 'point').

rejected_barriers.quote: their mother, the Sicel woman
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's words, read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: We have been wanting to begin for some time and have been waiting for you.
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's own sequence ('Then they began eating' … 'we have been wanting to begin'), not a slip of the modernization.

rejected_barriers.quote: Rumor went around the town
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's personification ('Rumour'), read correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: this man has done the Achaeans great wrong
rejected_barriers.reason: Ethnic names, kept unglossed by instruction.

rejected_barriers.quote: to Pylos or to Elis, where the Epeans rule
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's names. Not explained.

rejected_barriers.quote: Let us be up and doing
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's idiom, current if old-fashioned. Read correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: But Medon and the bard Phemius had now awakened
rejected_barriers.reason: Medon and Phemius are spared in Book 22, and Butler says no more here.

rejected_barriers.quote: take the form of Mentor
rejected_barriers.reason: Mentor, and Athena's use of his form, run from Book 2 on.

rejected_barriers.quote: check the folly of your sons, who were doing much wrong in the wantonness of their hearts
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's words, read correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: more than half raised a loud shout, and at once left the assembly
rejected_barriers.reason: Ruling: the modern does not depart from Butler anywhere that bears on the split. 'more than half … left the assembly. But the rest stayed … and they sided with Eupeithes. They therefore hurried off for their weapons' follows Butler clause for clause. Only his semicolon becomes a full stop, and his 'armour' becomes 'weapons'. The version the reader half-recalls is another translator's reading of the Greek.

rejected_barriers.quote: while we cause the others to forgive and forget
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's words, read correctly. The divine peace is the poem's and is not explained.

rejected_barriers.quote: see if they are not getting close up to us
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's idiom, which is still heard ('see if they aren't getting close'), and the next sentence resolves it ('he could see them all quite near'). Dropping 'not' would delete Butler's word.

rejected_barriers.quote: his three men
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's count, read correctly.

rejected_barriers.quote: Son of Arceisius
rejected_barriers.reason: Patronymic, kept by instruction. ¶15 gave it.

rejected_barriers.quote: pray to the blue-eyed maiden Athena
rejected_barriers.reason: Read correctly. For the record, Butler has 'pray to the blue-eyed damsel, and to Jove her father'; the name 'Athena' is the accepted text's addition. It prevents exactly the confusion the reader describes, so it is not proposed for removal, but it is noted for the verifier.

rejected_barriers.quote: poise your spear and hurl it
rejected_barriers.reason: 'poise' (hold balanced, ready to throw) is current ('poised to strike'). Read correctly with high confidence.

rejected_barriers.quote: the son of Cronus sent a thunderbolt of fire that fell just in front of Athena
rejected_barriers.reason: Patronymic (GLOSSARY 'son of Cronus'). What the bolt means is the poem's.

rejected_barriers.quote: Then Athena assumed the form and voice of Mentor
rejected_barriers.reason: Butler's words. Athena taking Mentor's form a second time is the poem's.

rejected_barriers.quote: presently made a covenant of peace
rejected_barriers.reason: Ruling: keep. In past narration 'presently' means 'soon after', as the reader glossed it, and 'covenant' is current. The abrupt divine peace is the poem's and is not explained.

recurring.rendering: Keep as printed. After a future verb (23.11, 'she will make up her mind about it presently') and in past narration (24.7, 24.44) it cannot be read as 'currently'. This is the tense rule the other Books' adjudications apply: kept at 4.57 and 10.44, changed only at the present-tense 4.8.
'grain' (B24-03), as 3.36 already prints ('the grain lands of the open country').
'did not know whether' (B24-01), as at 4.9. The other current Books print 'did not know what to do' (6.11) and 'was uncertain whether' (10.11), and none keeps 'doubted whether'.
'taller and sturdier' (B24-04), applied only together with the Book 8 adjudication's B08-01 at 8.1. Butler's different phrase 'taller and stronger' (23.15) stays.

Kept apart: 'slaves' for Butler's slaves (24.12, 24.15), and 'bondservant(s)' for his bondsmen and bondman (24.14, 24.15). 'bondservant(s)' is the edition's settled word (see the Book 4 adjudication).

Butler's own distinct nouns (needlework, pall, web, stitches, robe) are kept. 'Sweethearts' is kept too. The same speech recurs in Books 2 and 19, so any change to it would have to be made in all three places.
No change proposed. 24.0 prints the GLOSSARY's 'At that' and 24.29 prints 'at which'. Both read correctly; whether to make them agree is the lead's call, not a comprehension repair.

recurring.item: 'opened the gate(s) and sallied forth, Ulysses leading the way' (one Butler formula, used twice)
recurring.rendering: No comprehension repair is proposed, because the reader understood both. It is printed 'sallied forth' at 23.28 and 'marched out' at 24.37. If the lead wants one form, the choice is between restoring Butler's current-if-dated phrase at 24.37 (D29) and extending the accepted, plainer 'marched out' to 23.28.

recurring.item: Butler's 'try him' / 'make trial of' (= put to the test)
recurring.rendering: 'try' is kept at 23.17 (ruling). 24.14 already prints 'test' for 'make trial of'. 'test' is the fallback at 23.17 if the lead wants it.
'get about' at 23.27 (B23-04), Butler's own phrase for the same news at 23.13. 24.28 already prints 'spread news of' for Butler's 'noised abroad'.
Kept. The reader identified the great hall at every occurrence.
23.10's accepted 'in time' (future sense) stands. 24.25's 'By and by' is past narration and is kept, because 'in time' there would read as 'punctually'.
Comprehension is fine; this is a records note only. The GLOSSARY supplied here calls its Roman→Greek table closed and lists no Bacchus row, but 24.5 prints 'Dionysus' for Butler's 'Bacchus'.
Kept unglossed by instruction: son of Peleus, son of Atreus, daughter of Tyndareus, son of Arceisius, son of Cronus; Danaans, Argives, Achaeans, Cephallenians, Sicel, Epeans.

summary: Book 24 reads well: all 45 paraphrases match Butler, and the 83 barriers are overwhelmingly Butler's names, patronymics and ethnic names (kept unglossed by instruction), Trojan War and underworld backstory, the poem's own lies and abrupt peace, and dated idioms the reader glossed correctly. One repair is recommended: 'corn' (¶20), which this American-English edition turns into maize, becomes 'grain', as 3.36 already prints. Three are optional: two remove obsolete constructions that blur or can invert the sense ('not a single plant … but bears' at ¶15 becomes 'that does not bear', and 'He doubted whether' at ¶14 becomes 'did not know whether', as at 4.9), and 'stouter' becomes 'sturdier' at ¶23, only together with the Book 8 adjudication's B08-01 on the same Butler phrase. Ruled and kept: Amphimedon's 'quantity of iron … to be competed for' (Butler's words; the axes come from Books 19 and 21), the weaving nouns and 'Sweethearts' (Butler's; the speech recurs in Books 2 and 19), and 'presently'. The ¶32 assembly split follows Butler clause for clause, and nothing is blocking.
